etymology: From Saxon boc, a book, and also a beech tree, from the beechen boards on which the northern nations cut their letters. Hebrew sepher is anything written — a letter, a deed of sale, a scroll of the law — from saphar, to count, to recount, to number; the same root gives the word for scribe. What is written is what has been counted, and what has been counted is not lost.
biblical_def: A book in Scripture is a written thing that outlasts the man who wrote it, and the Bible's own claim is that God keeps books. Moses, pleading for a rebellious nation, appeals to one: “Yet now, if thou wilt forgive their sin—; and if not, blot me, I pray thee, out of thy book which thou hast written” (Exodus 32:32). David finds his own unformed body already entered in another: “in thy book all my members were written” (Psalm 139:16). A third is opened in a day when the faithful feared they had spoken to no purpose: “a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD” (Malachi 3:16). And the last vision of Scripture sets the books against the book: “the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life” (Revelation 20:12) — the record of works that condemns every man, and the register of grace that saves the elect. The word therefore carries two offices at once. It is the ordinary furniture of literate men, the deed and the letter and the scroll; and it is the figure under which God declares that nothing is forgotten, neither the sin He must judge nor the name He has written down in mercy. To have a book is to have a permanence that memory cannot supply, and that is exactly why God gave His church a book and not a tradition of talk.
webster_summary: A written or printed volume; anything committed to writing and preserved; in Scripture, the roll of the law, the register of a man's days, the book of remembrance kept for them that fear the LORD, and the book of life in which the names of the redeemed are written.
webster_full: BOOK, n. 1. A general name of every literary composition which is printed; but appropriately, a printed composition bound.
2. A particular part of a literary composition; a division of a subject in the same volume.
3. A volume or collection of sheets in which accounts are kept; a register of debts and credits.
4. From Saxon boc, a beech tree, the bark or boards of which were used by the northern nations for writing.
5. In Scripture, the book of the law, Deut. 31; the book of life, Rev. 20; a book of remembrance, Mal. 3.
corruption_summary: The book of life is emptied of its particularity and treated as a register of all mankind, or as a roll a man may write himself into and out of at will; and the written word itself is demoted beneath the living voice of the church or of private impression.
corruption_paragraphs: The book of life is the first casualty. Universalist readings make it a roll of the whole race, so that Revelation 20:15 threatens no one; Arminian readings make it a list from which names are entered and erased with the fluctuations of a man's will, so that God's writing is only a record of ours. Scripture will bear neither. The names in it were written from the foundation of the world (Revelation 13:8; 17:8), which is election in the plainest words the Spirit could use, and they were written by God, who does not learn and does not revise. Moses' plea in Exodus 32:32 is not a proof that names fall out of it but the intercession of a mediator offering himself in the place of the guilty — a shadow of the greater Mediator who was in fact blotted out of the land of the living for His people, that not one of theirs might be.

The second corruption is older and broader: the demotion of the written word beneath the unwritten. Rome sets an oral tradition beside the book and gives the magisterium the power to declare what the book means, so that in practice the book is read through the church rather than the church judged by the book. The charismatic wing of Protestantism does the same by another road, setting fresh impressions and prophecies beside the closed canon. Both forget why God gave a book at all. Speech dies with the speaker and is remembered as the hearer chooses; writing stands, is public, can be searched, and can convict the man who taught wrongly. That is why the Bereans could test an apostle, and why the LORD commanded the king to have his own copy in his own hand. A church that will not be judged by a book has arranged to be judged by nobody.
roots_summary: Hebrew sepher, a writing, letter, or scroll, from saphar, to count or recount; Greek biblion, a small roll, from biblos, the papyrus pith on which men wrote.
roots_lines: Hebrew sepher (H5612) — a written document of any kind: a bill of divorcement, a deed, a letter, the book of the law; over 180 occurrences.
Hebrew saphar (H5608) — to count, number, recount, declare; the root behind both sepher, a book, and sopher, a scribe.
Hebrew megillah (H4039) — a roll or volume; the roll Jehoiakim cut with the penknife and burned (Jeremiah 36:23).
Greek biblion (G975) — a small book or scroll; the book of life, and the little book John was given to eat (Revelation 10:9).
Greek biblos (G976) — the inner bark of the papyrus, hence a written scroll; “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ” (Matthew 1:1).
usage: Of the divine register of the redeemed: another book was opened, which is the book of life (Revelation 20:12).
Of God's knowledge of a man before his birth: in thy book all my members were written (Psalm 139:16).
Of the LORD's notice of quiet fidelity: a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD (Malachi 3:16).

Yet now, if thou wilt forgive their sin--; and if not, blot me, I pray thee, out of thy book which thou hast written.
Psalm 139:16
Thine eyes did see my substance, yet being unperfect; and in thy book all my members were written, which in continuance were fashioned, when as yet there was none of them.

etymology: From Saxon writan, to cut, to score, to engrave — the oldest sense is not ink but incision, the letter cut into stone or wood. Hebrew kathab and Greek graphō carry the same weight: to inscribe, to set down permanently. Our word Scripture is simply the passive of the Greek verb — the thing that has been written.
biblical_def: Writing is the act by which a word is fixed so that it cannot be quietly altered, and God is the first writer in Scripture: the tables of the testimony were “written with the finger of God” (Exodus 31:18). From that beginning the command to write runs through the whole Bible. Israel was to write the law where daily life would meet it: “And thou shalt write them upon the posts of thy house, and on thy gates” (Deuteronomy 6:9). Wisdom presses the same command inward, from doorpost to conscience: “bind them about thy neck; write them upon the table of thine heart” (Proverbs 3:3). The prophet is told to write so plainly that a man in motion can take it in: “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it” (Habakkuk 2:2). And the new covenant is defined by a writing God performs Himself in the place where no man can reach: “I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33). The progression is the doctrine. What God wrote on stone accused; what He writes on the heart of a regenerate man is the same law, now loved. Between the two stands the written Scripture, given because God intended His church to have a standard she could not amend by forgetting.
webster_summary: To form letters with a pen or by engraving; to set down permanently; in Scripture, God writing the law on tables of stone with His own finger, Israel commanded to write it on posts and gates, and the LORD promising to write His law in the hearts of His people.
webster_full: WRITE, v.t. 1. To form by a pen on paper or other material, or by a graver on wood or stone; to inscribe.
2. To express by letters; to compose; to produce as an author.
3. To engrave; to imprint; to impress durably.
4. From Saxon writan, to cut or score, the primary sense being to scratch or engrave.
5. In Scripture, written with the finger of God, Exod. 31; write them upon the table of thine heart, Prov. 3.
corruption_summary: Writing is treated as a merely human and culturally conditioned act, so that Scripture becomes a record of men's religious experience rather than a text God caused to be written; and the promised writing on the heart is read as making the written law obsolete.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern academic biblical scholarship begins from the assumption that the biblical books were assembled late by editors with agendas — a documentary hypothesis for the Torah, a school of disciples for the prophets, a community rather than an apostle behind the Gospels. On that assumption writing is only the sediment of a religious community's development, and the text's claims about its own origin are the first thing to be discounted. Scripture asserts the opposite at every turn: Moses wrote (Exodus 24:4; Deuteronomy 31:9), the prophets wrote at command, Paul wrote with his own hand, and the whole is God-breathed. Verbal plenary inspiration means the writing itself, and not merely the ideas behind it, is what God gave. Once that is denied, no doctrine is safe, because every hard text can be assigned to a later hand.

The second error takes Jeremiah 31:33 and turns it against the written word: if God writes His law on the heart, the argument runs, the external written law is superseded and the believer is guided by an inward sense. But Jeremiah does not say God will write a different law; He says He will write my law — the same commandments, now inscribed where the will is. The new covenant does not abolish the standard; it changes the man who meets it. The practical test is simple and searching. A heart truly written upon runs to the written word and finds it sweet, as Psalm 119 does for one hundred and seventy-six verses; a heart that appeals to an inward writing in order to escape a written command has confused the Spirit with itself.
roots_summary: Hebrew kathab, to write, inscribe, engrave; charath, to grave, used of the writing on the tables; Greek graphō, to write, whence graphē, a writing, the Scripture.
roots_lines: Hebrew kathab (H3789) — to write, record, enrol; used of God writing the commandments and of Moses writing the words of the LORD.
Hebrew charath (H2801) — to engrave; used once, of the writing graven upon the tables (Exodus 32:16).
Hebrew mikthab (H4385) — a writing, that which is written; “the writing was the writing of God” (Exodus 32:16).
Greek graphō (G1125) — to write; the perfect gegraptai, “it is written,” is our Lord's whole answer to the tempter.
Greek graphē (G1124) — a writing, and specifically the Scripture; “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2 Timothy 3:16).
usage: Of the household duty to publish the law: thou shalt write them upon the posts of thy house, and on thy gates (Deuteronomy 6:9).
Of the new covenant's inward work: I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts (Jeremiah 31:33).
Of plain prophetic publication: Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables (Habakkuk 2:2).

And thou shalt write them upon the posts of thy house, and on thy gates.
Proverbs 3:3

And the LORD answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it.

etymology: From Saxon raedan, to counsel, to discern, to read — the same root as our rede, counsel. Hebrew qara' means first to call or cry aloud, and reading in Israel was reading out; Greek anaginōskō is literally to know again, to recognise, since to read is to take back up a knowledge someone has already set down.
biblical_def: Reading in Scripture is a public and covenantal act before it is a private one. When the exiles returned, the great scene of reformation is a reading: “So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Nehemiah 8:8) — the text read out, and then explained, which is the whole pattern of preaching in one verse. The king of Israel was bound to the same discipline for himself: “he shall read therein all the days of his life: that he may learn to fear the LORD his God” (Deuteronomy 17:19) — the crown does not exempt a man from the book, it binds him to it. Our Lord kept the practice without apology: “as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, and stood up for to read” (Luke 4:16). And when a foreign official was found reading Isaiah in a chariot, the Spirit sent a preacher to him with one question: “Understandest thou what thou readest?” (Acts 8:30) — a question that assumes the text has a sense, that the sense can be missed, and that God supplies men to give it. To read the Scriptures is therefore not to gather information; it is to be summoned, and the fear of the LORD is the stated aim.
webster_summary: To peruse and understand written characters; to utter aloud what is written; in Scripture, the public reading of the law with the sense given, the king's daily reading that he might learn to fear the LORD, and the eunuch asked whether he understood what he read.
webster_full: READ, v.t. 1. To utter or pronounce written or printed words, letters or characters in the proper order.
2. To inspect and understand words or characters; to peruse silently.
3. To discover by marks; to understand; as, to read a man's countenance.
4. From Saxon raedan, to counsel, advise, discern; whence rede, counsel.
5. In Scripture, they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, Neh. 8; understandest thou what thou readest? Acts 8.
corruption_summary: Reading is redefined as an act in which the reader creates the meaning, so that the text has as many senses as it has readers; and against this, some react by denying that the sense ever needs to be given at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Postmodern literary theory teaches that a text has no fixed sense apart from the reader, and that every reading is finally an act of power. Reader-response criticism carried this into the church, where it now appears in the small-group question “what does this verse mean to you?” — a question that, taken seriously, abolishes the possibility of being wrong. Scripture assumes throughout that a text has a sense the reader is answerable to: Philip asks the eunuch, “Understandest thou what thou readest?” and the eunuch confesses that he cannot without a guide. Nehemiah 8:8 sets the standard against which the modern practice is measured — they read the text, and then they gave the sense, which presupposes that the text has one and that it can be missed. The Reformation principle of the plain sense is not naivety about difficulty; it is the confession that God spoke in order to be understood.

The opposite error deserves naming too, because it grows in reaction. Some insist that the plain reading is so plain that no teaching, no study of the original tongues, and no help from the church of past ages is needed, and that any explanation is a human addition. But God gave teachers as a gift to the church, and the same chapter that commands the reading commands that the sense be given. The principle to recover holds both together: the text is public, its sense is real and findable, and God has appointed men to open it — who are themselves to be tested by it, as the Bereans tested Paul.
roots_summary: Hebrew qara', to call, cry, proclaim, and so to read aloud; Greek anaginōskō, to know again, to read; anagnōsis, the public reading.
roots_lines: Hebrew qara' (H7121) — to call out, proclaim, name, and hence to read aloud; the ordinary word for public reading of the law.
Hebrew miqra' (H4744) — a calling together, a convocation, and in later Hebrew the Scripture itself as that which is read.
Greek anaginōskō (G314) — to read; literally to know again, to recognise what another has written.
Greek anagnōsis (G320) — the reading; “give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1 Timothy 4:13).
Aramaic qera' (H7123) — to read or call; used of the wise men who could not read the writing on Belshazzar's wall (Daniel 5:8).
usage: Of public reading with exposition: they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense (Nehemiah 8:8).
Of the ruler bound to the book: he shall read therein all the days of his life (Deuteronomy 17:19).
Of reading that needs a guide: Understandest thou what thou readest? (Acts 8:30).

etymology: From Latin recordari, to call to mind, from re-, again, and cor, cordis, the heart — to bring back to the heart. In the Authorized Version the noun and verb most often render the vocabulary of witness rather than of archives: to bear record is to testify, and a record is a testimony that will stand up when challenged.
biblical_def: In the Authorized Version record is chiefly a courtroom word. Job, abandoned by his friends and slandered in his affliction, appeals past them to a higher bench: “Also now, behold, my witness is in heaven, and my record is on high” (Job 16:19). Moses summons creation itself to the witness box: “I call heaven and earth to record this day against you, that I have set before you life and death” (Deuteronomy 30:19) — the covenant is not a private arrangement but a public deed with witnesses, and the witnesses outlive the generation that heard it. John the Baptist's ministry is summarised by the same word: “And this is the record of John, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, Who art thou?” (John 1:19) — a man whose entire office was to testify to Another. And the evangelist stakes the credibility of the crucifixion narrative on eyewitness testimony: “And he that saw it bare record, and his record is true” (John 19:35). The word therefore joins two things the modern mind separates: memory and evidence. A record is what is remembered because it was witnessed, set down where it can be produced. The gospel is preached in exactly this register — not as a religious sentiment but as sworn testimony to public events, which is why unbelief is treated as calling God a liar rather than as merely holding a different view.
webster_summary: A written memorial or authentic testimony; to bear witness, to testify; in Scripture, Job's record on high, heaven and earth called to record against Israel, the record of John the Baptist, and the eyewitness whose record of the crucifixion is true.
webster_full: RECORD, v.t. 1. To register; to enroll; to write or enter in a book for the purpose of preserving authentic evidence.
2. To imprint deeply on the mind or memory.
3. To testify; to bear witness. Acts 20.
4. From Latin recordor, to call to mind, from re and cor, the heart.
5. RECORD, n. An authentic memorial; a register; testimony borne. This is the record of John, John 1.
corruption_summary: The apostolic record is reclassified as the community's faith-memory rather than eyewitness testimony to events, so that the resurrection is preserved as meaning while being surrendered as fact.
corruption_paragraphs: The characteristic move of liberal and neo-orthodox theology is to keep the language of testimony while emptying it of the thing testified to. The Gospels, it is said, record not what happened but what the early community believed happened; the resurrection is the church's Easter faith rather than a body that walked out of a tomb. Bultmann's programme of demythologising made this explicit, and it survives in every treatment that calls the empty tomb a symbol. John will not permit it. He says, of a soldier's spear and the water and blood that followed, that the man who saw it bare record, and his record is true, and that he wrote it so that the reader might believe. That is the language of a deposition, not of a symbol. Paul argues the same way in 1 Corinthians 15: if Christ be not risen, the apostles are found false witnesses, which is a category that only applies where a factual claim was made.

The consequence is not academic. Testimony can be believed or disbelieved, but it cannot be reinterpreted without calling the witness a liar — and Scripture says as much: “he that believeth not God hath made him a liar; because he believeth not the record that God gave of his Son” (1 John 5:10). The principle to recover is the evidentiary character of Christian faith. God has not asked men to admire a story; He has produced witnesses, entered their testimony into a permanent record, and appointed a day in which the same record will be read back. Job's comfort is the believer's still: whatever the court of public opinion enters against him, his record is on high.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'ēd, a witness, and zikkarōn, a memorial or thing recorded; Greek martyria, testimony, and martyreō, to bear record.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'ēd (H5707) — a witness; the covenant word behind “I call heaven and earth to record” (Deuteronomy 30:19).
Hebrew zikkarōn (H2146) — a memorial, a remembrance written down; from zakar, to remember.
Greek martyria (G3141) — testimony, witness borne; the noun rendered record throughout John's Gospel and epistles.
Greek martyreō (G3140) — to bear witness, to testify; “he that saw it bare record” (John 19:35).
Greek martys (G3144) — a witness; the word from which martyr comes, since testimony under threat proved costly.
usage: Of the believer's appeal past human courts: my witness is in heaven, and my record is on high (Job 16:19).
Of covenant witnesses summoned: I call heaven and earth to record this day against you (Deuteronomy 30:19).
Of apostolic eyewitness: he that saw it bare record, and his record is true (John 19:35).

etymology: From French lettre, Latin litera, a written character, and thence a written message. Greek gramma is a written character from graphō, to write; in Paul's hands it becomes a technical term for the law considered simply as a written code confronting an unregenerate man.
biblical_def: The word means an alphabetic character, and a written message, and in Paul's letters it becomes a doctrine. In the ordinary sense he writes: “Ye see how large a letter I have written unto you with mine own hand” (Galatians 6:11) — the apostle taking the pen from the amanuensis to authenticate the whole. But he also uses the word for a living epistle: “Ye are our epistle written in our hearts, known and read of all men” (2 Corinthians 3:2) — converted men are the letter the ministry has written. Out of that comparison comes the great antithesis: “not of the letter, but of the spirit: for the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life” (2 Corinthians 3:6), and again, “we should serve in newness of spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter” (Romans 7:6). The letter here is not the words of Scripture as opposed to their meaning. It is the law as a written covenant of works, holy and just, standing over a dead man and pronouncing sentence; the spirit is the ministry of the new covenant in which the Holy Ghost writes that same law on a heart He has made alive. The law kills not because it is bad but because the sinner is; and the Spirit gives life not by lowering the standard but by raising the dead.
webster_summary: A mark or character used to represent an articulate sound; a written message sent from one person to another; and in Paul's doctrine the law as a written code that condemns, set over against the Spirit that gives life.
webster_full: LETTER, n. 1. A mark or character, written, printed or engraved, used as the representative of a sound.
2. A written message; an epistle. Letters are written on paper and sent by messenger or post.
3. The literal meaning; as, to adhere to the letter rather than the spirit of a law.
4. From Latin litera, a written character; French lettre.
5. In Scripture, the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life, 2 Cor. 3.
corruption_summary: “The letter killeth” is quoted to license loose handling of the text, as though careful attention to what is written were itself the deadly thing and impressions of the Spirit were the living alternative.
corruption_paragraphs: Few verses are wrenched further from their sense than 2 Corinthians 3:6. It is produced whenever a plain word of Scripture stands in the way — on divorce, on eldership, on the sexual ethic — with the claim that insisting on the letter is legalism and that the Spirit leads to a freer reading. Origen used it to justify allegory that dissolved the historical sense; medieval exegesis built four senses on the back of it; modern progressive readers use it to set the Spirit against the text on every disputed question. But Paul is contrasting two covenants, not two ways of reading. He names them: the ministration of death written and engraven in stones, and the ministration of the Spirit (2 Corinthians 3:7-8). The letter that kills is Sinai's law confronting a sinner without a Mediator; it is not exegetical care.

The tell is easy to read. A man appealing to the Spirit against the letter always finds that the Spirit agrees with him and disagrees with the text, and the disagreement always falls where the flesh was already uncomfortable. The Spirit who is set against the letter is never the Spirit who inspired it. The principle to recover is the one Paul actually teaches: the same Holy Ghost who breathed out the written word writes it on the heart, so that the believer's liberty consists in loving what the letter commands rather than in escaping it. A living epistle, known and read of all men, is a man in whom the written word has become visible — not a man who has left it behind.
roots_summary: Hebrew sepher, a written document or letter; Greek gramma, a written character or code, and epistolē, a letter sent.
roots_lines: Greek gramma (G1121) — a letter of the alphabet, a writing, and in Paul the law as written code (Romans 2:27; 7:6).
Greek epistolē (G1992) — a letter sent, an epistle; “Ye are our epistle written in our hearts” (2 Corinthians 3:2).
Greek pneuma (G4151) — spirit, breath; the Holy Ghost set over against the gramma in 2 Corinthians 3:6.
Hebrew sepher (H5612) — a written document; the letter Sennacherib sent and Hezekiah spread before the LORD (Isaiah 37:14).
Hebrew 'iggereth (H107) — a letter, dispatch; the letters of Purim sent to all the Jews (Esther 9:29).
usage: Of the two covenants contrasted: the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life (2 Corinthians 3:6).
Of converted men as the minister's credential: Ye are our epistle written in our hearts, known and read of all men (2 Corinthians 3:2).
Of apostolic authentication: Ye see how large a letter I have written unto you with mine own hand (Galatians 6:11).

etymology: A verbal noun from say, Saxon secgan, to utter. In the Authorized Version a saying is a definite utterance treated as a unit — a word that can be kept, pondered, believed, or rejected as a whole, and which is often quoted back later because it was remembered.
biblical_def: A saying in Scripture is a word that has been fixed in the memory and can be handed on. Mary's response to what she could not yet understand is the model: “his mother kept all these sayings in her heart” (Luke 2:51) — not solved, not explained, kept. The Lord Jesus closes the Sermon on the Mount by making His sayings the foundation a life is built on or ruined for want of: “whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man” (Matthew 7:24). John records how a saying can travel and be corrupted in transit: “Then went this saying abroad among the brethren, that that disciple should not die: yet Jesus said not unto him” (John 21:23) — the report circulated, and the evangelist corrects it by returning to what was actually said. And Paul stamps five sayings in the Pastorals with an apostolic seal, of which the first is the sum of the gospel: “This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners” (1 Timothy 1:15). These faithful sayings are the earliest confessional formulae of the church — compact, memorable, doctrinally exact — and they show that the apostolic church catechised by fixed forms of sound words, not by impressions.
webster_summary: An expression, a declaration, a maxim uttered and remembered; in Scripture, the sayings of Christ that a wise man builds upon, the sayings Mary kept in her heart, and the faithful sayings the apostle stamps as worthy of all acceptation.
webster_full: SAYING, n. 1. An expression; a sentence uttered; a declaration.
2. A proverbial expression; a maxim; as, it is a common saying.
3. That which is repeated and remembered as the word of another.
4. From say, Saxon secgan, to utter, to speak.
5. In Scripture, a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptation, 1 Tim. 1; his mother kept all these sayings in her heart, Luke 2.
corruption_summary: The sayings of Christ are separated from His person and His atoning work, so that He is honoured as a teacher of maxims while the doctrine that gives the maxims their force is quietly dropped.
corruption_paragraphs: Nineteenth-century liberalism produced a Jesus who was a teacher of timeless sayings and little else — the Sermon on the Mount without the cross, the golden rule without the wrath it saves from. The same instinct persists wherever the words of Christ are printed in red and treated as the real gospel while the epistles that expound His death are treated as Paul's overlay. But the Lord's sayings will not survive the separation. Matthew 7:24 makes obedience to His sayings the difference between a house that stands and one that falls, and the sentence is a claim to divine authority that no mere teacher could make. Strip out who He is and the sayings become an intolerable moral burden, which is exactly what they were designed to be for the self-righteous and never were for those who came to Him poor in spirit.

The opposite corruption is the endless multiplication of sayings that God never said. John 21:23 is instructive because it shows how quickly a report can circulate among believers in a form the Lord never uttered, and how an apostle handles it — not by celebrating the tradition but by correcting it against the actual words. The modern equivalents are the “God told me” culture of the charismatic movement and the pious slogans that circulate as though they were scripture. The principle to recover is the apostolic one: fixed, faithful sayings, tested and confessed, held fast in the form of sound words, and everything else measured by them.
roots_summary: Hebrew dabar, a word or matter spoken; 'imrah, an utterance or speech; Greek logos, a word or discourse, and rhēma, a spoken saying.
roots_lines: Hebrew dabar (H1697) — a word, saying, or matter; the same noun covers the thing said and the thing done.
Hebrew 'imrah (H565) — an utterance, speech, commandment; frequent in Psalm 119 for God's word as promise.
Greek logos (G3056) — a word, account, or discourse; rendered saying where a definite utterance is in view.
Greek rhēma (G4487) — a spoken word, a saying; “they understood not this saying” (Luke 9:45).
Greek pistos ho logos — “faithful is the word,” the apostolic formula introducing the five faithful sayings of the Pastorals.
usage: Of the gospel in one confessional sentence: This is a faithful saying... that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners (1 Timothy 1:15).
Of the foundation of an obedient life: whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them (Matthew 7:24).
Of a report corrected against the actual word: yet Jesus said not unto him (John 21:23).

This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.
Matthew 7:24
Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock:
Luke 2:51
And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject unto them: but his mother kept all these sayings in her heart.
John 21:23
Then went this saying abroad among the brethren, that that disciple should not die: yet Jesus said not unto him, He shall not die; but, If I will that he tarry till I come, what is that to thee?

etymology: From Latin materia, stuff, substance, and thence the subject of a discourse or a case at law. In the Authorized Version it usually renders Hebrew dabar — the same noun that means word — because in Hebrew a thing said and a thing done are one vocabulary; a matter is a word that has become a case.
biblical_def: A matter is an affair requiring judgment, and Scripture treats the handling of matters as a moral test. Jethro's counsel establishes the pattern of judicial order in Israel: “every great matter they shall bring unto thee, but every small matter they shall judge” (Exodus 18:22) — graduated courts, competent men, and no one crushed under a docket he cannot carry. Wisdom governs the tongue in matters that belong to another: “A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter” (Proverbs 11:13). Peter uses the word to shut a man out of a ministry he had tried to purchase: “Thou hast neither part nor lot in this matter: for thy heart is not right in the sight of God” (Acts 8:21) — the matter is the gospel ministry itself, and the disqualification is of the heart, not of the credentials. And the Preacher, having surveyed everything under the sun, brings all matters to one: “Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man” (Ecclesiastes 12:13). That verse is the dictionary's answer to every question of proportion. Matters are real, they must be judged, and they are all finally subordinate to a single account rendered to God.
webster_summary: The subject of a discourse or a case requiring decision; an affair, business, or cause at law; in Scripture, great matters and small brought before appointed judges, the matter a faithful man conceals, and the conclusion of the whole matter — fear God, and keep his commandments.
webster_full: MATTER, n. 1. Substance excluded from mind and spirit; body; that which is corporeal.
2. Subject; the thing treated; that about which we write or speak.
3. Affair; business; event; the cause in question; as, this is a serious matter.
4. From Latin materia, stuff, materials, the subject of discourse.
5. In Scripture, every great matter they shall bring unto thee, Exod. 18; the conclusion of the whole matter, Eccl. 12.
corruption_summary: Every matter is flattened to the same weight, so that trifles are prosecuted as though they were heresies and heresies excused as though they were trifles; and the Christian is taught to treat all opinion as a cause.
corruption_paragraphs: The discipline of proportion has largely collapsed. In an age of instant publication, every disagreement can be broadcast, and the incentives reward heat rather than weight, so that matters of indifference are pressed as tests of fellowship while genuine departures from the faith are waved through as matters of emphasis. Exodus 18:22 assumes exactly the opposite: that matters differ in gravity, that they are to be judged at the level proper to them, and that a man who brings every small matter to the highest court will wear out both himself and the court. The Reformed tradition captured this in the distinction between fundamental articles and things indifferent — not to make doctrine negotiable, but so that the church's discipline should fall where Scripture makes it fall.

The second failure is the tongue. Proverbs 11:13 names the talebearer, and the modern forms are efficient beyond anything Solomon knew: the group message, the anonymous account, the screenshot forwarded with a note of concern. Where a matter belongs to another and no duty requires disclosure, the faithful man conceals it. This is not secrecy about sin — the Lord Jesus gives a clear procedure for that in Matthew 18, and it begins between two, precisely so that a matter can be settled without an audience. What Proverbs forbids is the appetite for other men's business, dressed as candour. The Preacher's conclusion governs the whole: fear God, and keep His commandments, and most matters shrink to their proper size.
roots_summary: Hebrew dabar, a word, thing, or matter; Aramaic millah, a word or affair; Greek pragma, a thing done, a business or lawsuit, and logos, an account.
roots_lines: Hebrew dabar (H1697) — word, thing, matter, cause; the single noun covering speech and the affair it concerns.
Hebrew riyb (H7379) — a strife or legal contention; the matter brought before judges (Deuteronomy 17:8).
Aramaic millah (H4406) — a word, matter, or affair; frequent in Daniel for the king's matter and the dream.
Greek pragma (G4229) — a deed, thing, or business; used of a lawsuit between brethren (1 Corinthians 6:1).
Greek logos (G3056) — word, account, reckoning; rendered matter where a cause to be answered is meant (Acts 8:21).
usage: Of judicial proportion: every great matter they shall bring unto thee, but every small matter they shall judge (Exodus 18:22).
Of the discreet tongue: he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter (Proverbs 11:13).
Of the sum of all things: Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments (Ecclesiastes 12:13).

etymology: From French charger, to load, from Late Latin carricare, to load a wagon, from carrus, a cart. A charge is therefore something laid upon a man as a load he must carry. Hebrew mishmereth is from shamar, to keep or guard — a charge is a watch entrusted, a post one may not leave.
biblical_def: A charge is a duty laid on a man by one who has the right to lay it. Abraham is commended in these terms: “Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws” (Genesis 26:5). The Levites were given a charge in the strict sense of a watch — “they shall keep all the instruments of the tabernacle of the congregation, and the charge of the children of Israel” (Numbers 3:8) — a guard duty at the holy things, where negligence was not an administrative failure but a capital one. Paul lays the same weight on Timothy twice, and both times in the most solemn form the language allows: “I charge thee before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, and the elect angels, that thou observe these things without preferring one before another” (1 Timothy 5:21); and “I charge thee therefore before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, who shall judge the quick and the dead at his appearing and his kingdom” (2 Timothy 4:1) — the charge that precedes preach the word. And the word is used of God's own commission of His servants to guard His people: “he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways” (Psalm 91:11). In every case a charge is received, not chosen; it is answerable to the one who gave it; and it is kept by watchfulness rather than by enthusiasm.
webster_summary: That which is laid on or entrusted; a command or injunction solemnly given; the care or custody of something; in Scripture, the charge Abraham kept, the Levites' charge at the tabernacle, and the charge before God and the Lord Jesus Christ under which a minister preaches.
webster_full: CHARGE, v.t. 1. To lay on or impose, as a load, a task, a duty; to entrust.
2. To enjoin; to command; to exhort with authority. 1 Tim. 5.
3. To accuse; to lay to the charge of; to impute as a fault.
4. From French charger, to load, from Latin carrus, a cart or wagon.
5. In Scripture, kept my charge, Gen. 26; he shall give his angels charge over thee, Ps. 91.
corruption_summary: The pastoral charge is recast as a career with a job description, so that the minister answers to a board, a market, or his own gifting, rather than to the God before whom Paul charged Timothy in view of the judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: Where the ministry is understood as a profession, the charge quietly becomes a contract. The man is hired for competencies, reviewed against metrics, and released when the numbers fall; and because the pressure is real, his preaching bends toward what keeps the room full. Paul's formula was constructed to make that impossible. He charges Timothy before God and the Lord Jesus Christ, who shall judge the quick and the dead, at His appearing and His kingdom — four clauses that put the whole of a man's ministry under the eye of the Judge before whom he will stand. Then, and only then, comes the content of the charge: preach the word, be instant in season, out of season. A minister who has genuinely received that charge is unable to treat his pulpit as a platform he owns.

The Levitical picture supplies the other half. A charge in the Old Testament is a watch, a post, a guarded trust; the Levites were not creative about the tabernacle's furniture but faithful with it. So the elder is a steward of a deposit, charged to keep that which is committed to his trust (1 Timothy 6:20) — which means the doctrine he preaches is not his to improve. Both errors of the age fail this test: the man who trims the deposit to fit the culture, and the man who adds to it out of his own visions. The principle to recover is that the charge is given, not invented, and that keeping it is the whole of the office.
roots_summary: Hebrew mishmereth, a watch, guard, or charge kept, from shamar, to keep; Greek paraggellō, to pass an order along the line, and parangelia, the charge so given.
roots_lines: Hebrew mishmereth (H4931) — a watch, guard, obligation, or charge; the standing term for priestly and Levitical duty.
Hebrew shamar (H8104) — to keep, guard, observe; the root that makes a charge a thing watched rather than merely performed.
Greek paraggellō (G3853) — to transmit a message, to command; a military word for orders passed down from the commander.
Greek parangelia (G3852) — the charge or injunction given; “the end of the commandment is charity” (1 Timothy 1:5).
Greek diamartyromai (G1263) — to charge solemnly, to testify earnestly; the verb of 2 Timothy 4:1.
usage: Of the solemn ministerial commission: I charge thee therefore before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, who shall judge the quick and the dead (2 Timothy 4:1).
Of covenant fidelity in the patriarch: Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge (Genesis 26:5).
Of God's appointed guardians: he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways (Psalm 91:11).

I charge thee before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, and the elect angels, that thou observe these things without preferring one before another, doing nothing by partiality.
2 Timothy 4:1
I charge thee therefore before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, who shall judge the quick and the dead at his appearing and his kingdom;
Psalm 91:11
For he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways.
Genesis 26:5
Because that Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws.

etymology: From Saxon tidan, to happen or betide — tidings are literally the things that have betided, news of what has occurred. The Hebrew besorah is the report a runner carries from a battle, and the reward paid for bringing it; the Greek verb euangelizomai, to bring good tidings, is the root of our word gospel.
biblical_def: Tidings are news from a field a man could not see for himself, brought by a runner who was there. The word's natural home is the battlefield: “And, behold, Cushi came; and Cushi said, Tidings, my lord the king: for the LORD hath avenged thee this day of all them that rose up against thee” (2 Samuel 18:31). Isaiah takes that scene and makes it the picture of gospel preaching: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace” (Isaiah 52:7); and again, “O Zion, that bringest good tidings, get thee up into the high mountain” (Isaiah 40:9) — the herald is to climb where he can be heard and to lift up his voice with strength. The angel over Bethlehem uses precisely this vocabulary: “behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people” (Luke 2:10). The doctrine is in the grammar. Tidings are announced, not negotiated; they concern something already accomplished elsewhere; and the hearer's part is to believe the report, since he was not at the battle. So the gospel is not advice about how to be saved but news that a victory has been won, and preaching is the runner's office — to say accurately what happened, and to say it where men are.
webster_summary: News; account of what has happened; in Scripture, the runner's report from the battle, the good tidings published on the mountains by him whose feet are beautiful, and the angel's good tidings of great joy at the birth of Christ.
webster_full: TIDINGS, n. plu. 1. News; advice; information; intelligence; account of what has taken place.
2. That which betides or happens; hence, report of an event.
3. Good tidings, glad news; the annunciation of a benefit received or approaching.
4. From Saxon tidan, to happen, to betide; tid, time, season.
5. In Scripture, the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, Isa. 52; I bring you good tidings of great joy, Luke 2.
corruption_summary: The gospel is converted from news into advice — a programme of principles, a therapy, or a summons to social transformation — so that what Christ finished is replaced by what the hearer is to attempt.
corruption_paragraphs: News and advice call for different responses, and the distinction is where most modern preaching fails. Advice tells a man what to do; news tells him what has been done. When the pulpit offers steps to a better marriage, keys to victorious living, or a programme of civic renewal, it may be offering true things, but it is not bringing tidings, and the hearer goes home with a task rather than a Saviour. Isaiah's herald has no advice at all: he publishes peace, he publishes salvation, he says unto Zion, Thy God reigneth. Paul quotes that very verse in Romans 10 to define preaching, and immediately adds that faith cometh by hearing — which only makes sense if what is preached is a report to be believed.

The same substitution happens on the other flank when the gospel is reduced to a therapeutic message about acceptance. Here the news is not replaced by duty but by reassurance, and the cross becomes a demonstration of how much God values the hearer rather than the propitiation of His wrath against the hearer's sin. The angel's tidings at Bethlehem contain the correction: the joy is announced because a Saviour is born, which presupposes a peril the hearer cannot escape. The principle to recover is the runner's discipline — report what actually happened at the field, in the words of Him who sent you, and let the news do its own work.
roots_summary: Hebrew besorah, tidings or the reward for bringing them, from basar, to bear news; Greek euangelizomai, to announce good tidings, and euangelion, the good news itself.
roots_lines: Hebrew basar (H1319) — to bear tidings, to publish, to preach good news; the verb of Isaiah 52:7 and 40:9.
Hebrew besorah (H1309) — tidings, and also the reward given to the messenger (2 Samuel 4:10).
Greek euangelizomai (G2097) — to bring or announce good tidings; the verb the angel uses at Luke 2:10.
Greek euangelion (G2098) — good news, the gospel; the noun formed from eu, well, and angellō, to announce.
Greek kērussō (G2784) — to herald, to proclaim as a public crier; the office that carries the tidings (Romans 10:14).
usage: Of the preacher's beautiful feet: him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace (Isaiah 52:7).
Of the nativity announcement: I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people (Luke 2:10).
Of the runner from the battle: Tidings, my lord the king: for the LORD hath avenged thee this day (2 Samuel 18:31).

etymology: From Saxon thoht, from thencan, to think. Hebrew machashabah is from chashab, to weave, to devise, to reckon — a thought is something plaited together in the mind, a design; the same root is used of the skilled workman's cunning work in the tabernacle, so that a thought is a piece of interior craftsmanship, for good or ill.
biblical_def: Scripture treats thought as the first field of moral action, fully open to God and never neutral. David states the doctrine of divine omniscience in terms of it: “thou understandest my thought afar off” (Psalm 139:2) — before it is spoken, before it is fully formed, before the man himself has taken its measure. The verdict on fallen thought is unsparing: “The LORD knoweth the thoughts of man, that they are vanity” (Psalm 94:11), and the diagnosis before the flood reaches deeper still, that every imagination of the thoughts of man's heart was only evil continually. Our Lord addresses another kind of thought — anxious calculation about tomorrow: “Which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature?” (Matthew 6:27), where the King James take no thought means not carelessness but the corroding forecast that tries to carry a providence God has not yet given. And Paul assigns the mind to the field of war: “bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:5). Note the metaphor: thoughts are not merely disciplined, they are taken prisoner. Sanctification reaches the interior life or it has not begun; a man is what he thinks when no one is watching, and God is always watching.
webster_summary: The act or product of thinking; an idea, design, or purpose formed in the mind; also anxious care. In Scripture, the thoughts of man are vanity, the LORD understands them afar off, and every thought is to be brought into captivity to the obedience of Christ.
webster_full: THOUGHT, n. 1. The operation of the mind; the act of thinking; also, the idea produced.
2. Design; purpose; intention formed within.
3. Solicitude; anxious care. Take no thought for your life, Matt. 6.
4. From Saxon thoht, the participle of thencan, to think.
5. In Scripture, the LORD knoweth the thoughts of man, that they are vanity, Ps. 94; bringing into captivity every thought, 2 Cor. 10.
corruption_summary: The inner life is declared private and therefore morally exempt, so that sin is measured only by action and injury; and where thought is taken seriously it is handed to technique — positive thinking, self-talk, mindfulness — rather than to repentance and the renewing of the mind.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern moral reasoning locates guilt in the harm an act does to another, which leaves the thoughts of the heart outside the jurisdiction altogether. On that reckoning covetousness is not sin until it steals and lust is not sin until it acts. Our Lord's exposition of the law in Matthew 5 was aimed precisely at this evasion: the man who looks to lust hath committed adultery already in his heart, and the murderer's guilt begins in the anger that despises a brother. The tenth commandment is the same test in the Decalogue itself — a commandment no external code could enforce, given so that no man could think himself clean. Psalm 139:2 removes the last hiding place: the thought is understood afar off, and there is no interior room where God is not.

Where thought is taken seriously, the age hands it to technique. Positive-thinking religion, from Peale forward, promises that the mind can be trained to speak prosperity into being; the mindfulness industry, in its therapeutic form, teaches detachment from thoughts rather than repentance of them. Both leave the will untouched. Paul's language is warfare and captivity, not calm observation: the strong holds are pulled down, the imaginations are cast down, the thought is dragged in chains to the obedience of Christ. And the positive half is equally definite — the mind is renewed (Romans 12:2) and filled with whatsoever things are true, honest, just, pure, lovely and of good report (Philippians 4:8). The remedy for a corrupt thought-life is not a technique but a new master.
roots_summary: Hebrew machashabah, a device or purpose, from chashab, to weave or reckon; Greek noēma, a mental perception or device, and dialogismos, an inward reasoning.
roots_lines: Hebrew machashabah (H4284) — a thought, device, plan; also the skilled design of the tabernacle's cunning work.
Hebrew chashab (H2803) — to weave, devise, reckon, impute; the root behind both thought and imputation.
Greek noēma (G3540) — a perception, purpose, or device of the mind; “we are not ignorant of his devices” (2 Corinthians 2:11).
Greek dialogismos (G1261) — an inward reasoning or disputation; “the Lord knoweth the thoughts of the wise” (1 Corinthians 3:20).
Greek merimnaō (G3309) — to be anxious, to take thought; the verb behind “take no thought” in Matthew 6.
usage: Of divine omniscience: thou understandest my thought afar off (Psalm 139:2).
Of the futility of fallen reasoning: The LORD knoweth the thoughts of man, that they are vanity (Psalm 94:11).
Of the warfare of sanctification: bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ (2 Corinthians 10:5).
